h1: Olive Oil Smoke Point: What Heat It Can Actually Take
excerpt: The olive oil smoke point is a range rather than a fixed number, and freshness moves it more than the grade on the label does.
keyTakeaway: The olive oil smoke point is a range, not a number: roughly 190 to 210°C for extra virgin, higher for refined grades. Freshness and free fatty acid content move it more than the label does. Tumis, roasting and shallow-frying stay under it; a long deep-fry and a hard wok flame do not.
heroAlt: A Malaysian man in a black songkok, seated at a wooden bench, nosing olive oil from a cobalt-blue tasting glass, with a glass flask of oil, a rack of sample tubes and a microscope on the bench and olive branches behind him.
inlineAlt: Close view of the tasting bench: a hand holding a cobalt-blue tasting glass at the top left, a glass flask of yellow-green olive oil and a row of empty sample tubes in front of a microscope.
intro: Smoke point is the temperature at which an oil stops sitting quietly in the pan and starts giving off a steady haze. For extra virgin olive oil the figure gets repeated with a confidence nobody should have, because it is not one number. It is a range, and the range moves.
Here are the approximate figures for the olive oil grades and for the oils a Malaysian kitchen already keeps, what moves the number, and which everyday methods stay under it.

sections.heading: What a smoke point actually is

blocks.text: A smoke point is the temperature at which an oil begins to give off a continuous visible haze instead of a clean shimmer. What you are watching is the smallest, most volatile parts of the oil breaking away first. It is not a cliff edge: the aroma flattens well before anything smokes, which is why it matters more for extra virgin.

sections.heading: Olive oil smoke point figures, and how they compare

blocks.text: Published figures put extra virgin olive oil at roughly 190 to 210°C, with refined grades higher, because refining strips out the compounds that break down first. Read every figure below as an approximate range for the category, not a reading taken from your own bottle.

sections.heading: Freshness moves the number more than the grade does

blocks.text: Free fatty acids break down first, and an oil gathers them as it ages and as air, light and warmth work on it. A fresh, low-acidity extra virgin oil takes more heat than a tired one that has stood open beside the stove since March. The grade on the label describes a starting condition.

items: **Time.** Every month an opened bottle spends in a warm kitchen moves it the same way.
**Light.** Clear glass on a bright shelf ages an oil faster than dark glass in a cupboard.
**Air.** A half-empty bottle is half full of air, and the oil reacts with it.
**Reuse.** Oil already fried in starts lower.

sections.heading: Which Malaysian cooking methods stay under it

blocks.text: Most of what happens in a Malaysian kitchen sits comfortably inside the range. Tumis over a moderate flame runs near 120 to 160°C once the pan is loaded, and oven roasting at 180 to 200°C is fine. What goes past it is a long deep-fry and wok work on a hard flame.

items: Tumis for a rempah, onions or garlic: inside the range, and the oil carries the aromatics.
Roasting vegetables or chicken at 180 to 200°C: inside the range.
Shallow-frying fish or telur mata: inside it, unless the pan is left dry and smoking between batches.
A long deep-fry of pisang goreng or keropok: past it, and costly by the litre.
Wok on a full flame: past it, well past it.

blocks.text: Olive oil is a pan oil with a ceiling, and most home cooking sits below it. For where it fits across a week of meals, read [how to cook with olive oil in a Malaysian kitchen](/blog/how-to-cook-with-olive-oil-in-a-malaysian-kitchen).

sections.heading: How to tell when the oil has gone past it

blocks.text: You do not need a thermometer, because the pan tells you. A thin continuous haze lifting off the surface, a sharp smell where a fruity one was, and oil that has gone thin and runs too freely are the three signals. A shimmer is normal. Steady smoke means you are late.

items: Take the pan off the heat and give it thirty seconds before adding anything.
If it smoked hard, tip that oil out rather than cook in it.
Add the ingredients sooner: cold food drops the temperature at once.
Never leave a pan of oil heating while you chop.

sections.heading: Is reheating the oil worth it?

blocks.text: At **RM236 a litre** for the 250 ml bottle, filling a pot with extra virgin oil and straining it to use again is a poor trade. Each round leaves the oil darker, thicker and quieter in the nose, and lower than it was. Keep a cheap oil for volume frying and the extra virgin for the pan.
A better habit: cook with a modest amount, then finish the plate with a drizzle off the heat. The heated oil cooks, the raw oil carries the flavour.

Extra virgin sits around 190 to 210°C, refined grades higher, and a fresh bottle takes more heat than an old one. Tumis, roast and shallow-fry in it. Leave the long deep-fry and the roaring wok to something cheaper.

faqs.q: What is the smoke point of extra virgin olive oil?
faqs.a: Published ranges put it around 190 to 210°C. The figure depends on how fresh the oil is and how low its free fatty acid content is.

faqs.q: Can I fry with extra virgin olive oil?
faqs.a: Shallow-frying and pan-frying sit inside the range. A long deep-fry on a hard flame does not, and at RM236 a litre it is an expensive way to fill a pot.

faqs.q: Does refined olive oil have a higher smoke point?
faqs.a: Yes. Refining removes the free fatty acids and aromatic compounds that break down first, which lifts the figure and takes the flavour with it.

faqs.q: What happens to the flavour when olive oil smokes?
faqs.a: It flattens. The fruit and pepper go first and the food picks that up. If a pan has smoked hard, tip the oil out.

faqs.q: Why does olive oil smoke in my wok?
faqs.a: A wok on a full flame clears 250°C before anything is added, above the range for any olive oil. Use a lower flame, or another oil for wok work.

faqs.q: Does storing the bottle well change the smoke point?
faqs.a: Indirectly. Warmth, light and air raise free fatty acid content over time, so a bottle kept dark, capped and away from the stove holds its tolerance longer.
